questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. What does the expected effective service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=\mathbb{E}[S_0]+\mathbb{E}[R]/B$ of a single job measure?
options: The expected time from a job's arrival until it leaves, setup included.
The expected time from the start of its batch's setup until the job leaves.
The server time one job costs: its own service plus a $1/B$ share of the setup.
The expected service time of a whole batch: one setup and $B$ net services.

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B\geq2$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Jobs arrive at rate $\lambda$ and $S_B$ is the service time of a batch. Which expression equals the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$, with $S$ the effective service time per job?
options: $\lambda_B\mathbb{E}[S_B]$ with $\lambda_B=\lambda/B$, the batch rate times the batch work
$\lambda\mathbb{E}[S_B]$, the job arrival rate times the batch work
$\lambda_B\mathbb{E}[S]$ with $\lambda_B=\lambda/B$, the batch rate times the per-job work
$\lambda\mathbb{E}[S_0]+\lambda\mathbb{E}[R]$, the net load plus a full setup per job

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Jobs arrive at rate $\lambda>0$ and $\mathbb{E}[R]>0$. How does the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S_0]+\lambda\mathbb{E}[R]/B$ depend on the batch size $B$?
options: It increases in $B$, since every batch carries more work.
It does not depend on $B$, since the net work per job is fixed.
It first decreases and then increases in $B$, with a minimum.
It decreases strictly in $B$, towards the net load $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S_0]$.

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. The setup time $R$ is replaced by a setup with the same mean but a larger variance, while $B$ and $S_0$ stay the same. How do the effective service time's mean $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ change?
options: Both $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ increase.
Only $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ increases; $\mathbb{E}[S]$ stays the same.
$\mathbb{E}[S]$ increases, while $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ is unaffected.
Neither changes, since the setup is spread over $B$ jobs.

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Jobs of family $i$ arrive at rate $\lambda_i$ and are collected into batches of their own colour. A larger $B$ lowers the load. Why can it still raise a job's expected sojourn time?
options: A larger $B$ raises every job's setup share $\mathbb{E}[R]/B$.
A larger $B$ means more setups per hour, which adds work.
A job waits longer for its batch to form, $\frac{B-1}{2\lambda_i}$ on average.
A larger $B$ pushes the load $\rho$ closer to $1$, so queues grow.

questions.question: A machine serves jobs in batches of $B=6$: one setup with mean $\mathbb{E}[R]=30$ minutes, then six net services with mean $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=10$ minutes each. How much server time does one job cost on average, that is, its effective service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: $\tfrac{20}{3}\approx6.7$ minutes
$15$ minutes
$40$ minutes
$90$ minutes

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Jobs arrive at $\lambda=4$ per hour, $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=0.15$ hour, $\mathbb{E}[R]=0.5$ hour and $B=8$, so the server is stable. What long-run fraction of time does the server spend on setups?

In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Jobs arrive at $\lambda=2$ per hour, $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=0.3$ hour and $\mathbb{E}[R]=1.2$ hours. What is the smallest integer batch size $B$ with load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$?

Batches of $B=4$ jobs each need one setup $R$ with $\operatorname{Var}(R)=100$ minutes$^2$ and four i.i.d. net services $S_0$ with $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)=9$ minutes$^2$, independent of $R$. What is the variance $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ of the effective service time per job?
options: $109$ minutes$^2$
$25$ minutes$^2$
$34$ minutes$^2$
$136$ minutes$^2$

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Jobs arrive at $\lambda=5$ per hour, $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=10$ minutes, $\mathbb{E}[R]=40$ minutes and $B=10$. What is the load $\rho$, and can the server keep up?
options: $\rho\approx0.83$: the net work leaves spare capacity
$\rho\approx0.12$: the server is idle most of the time
$\rho\approx4.17$: overloaded more than fourfold
$\rho\approx1.17$: the server cannot keep up

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Jobs arrive at rate $\lambda$, $\mathbb{E}[R]>0$, and the net load already satisfies $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S_0]\geq1$. Which statement about stabilising the server by the choice of $B$ is correct?
options: Any $B>B_m=\lambda\mathbb{E}[R]/(1-\lambda\mathbb{E}[S_0])$ makes the load below $1$.
No $B$ works: $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S_0]+\lambda\mathbb{E}[R]/B$ exceeds $1$ for every $B$.
A large enough $B$ works, as the setup share $\lambda\mathbb{E}[R]/B$ tends to $0$.
A deterministic setup works, since then $\operatorname{Var}(S)=\operatorname{Var}(S_0)$ for every $B$.

questions.question: In a model where jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs with i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, the setup takes no time, $R=0$. Jobs of family $i$ arrive at rate $\lambda_i$ and form batches of their own colour. What does the choice of $B$ then change?
options: Not $\mathbb{E}[S]$ or the load; a larger $B$ only adds batch formation time.
The load still falls like $1/B$, so large batches still pay off.
$\mathbb{E}[S]$ grows with $B$, since each batch now holds more jobs.
Nothing: without setups every $B$ gives the same expected sojourn time.

questions.question: A machine serves batches of $B\geq2$ jobs: one setup $R$, then $B$ i.i.d. net services $S_0$. Jobs arrive at rate $\lambda$ with inter-arrival SCV $C_a^2$. Inserting $\lambda$, $C_a^2$ and the effective $\mathbb{E}[S]$, $C_s^2$ into Sakasegawa's one-server formula $\frac{C_a^2+C_s^2}{2}\cdot\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\cdot\mathbb{E}[S]$, $\rho<1$, approximates which quantity?
options: The expected sojourn time of a job, since $S$ already contains the setup
The expected time from a job's arrival until its own service starts
$\mathbb{E}[W_B]/B$, the batch queue time shared over the jobs of a batch
The expected time $\mathbb{E}[W_B]$ a complete batch waits in the queue

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. A batch with $B=5$ has $\mathbb{E}[S_B]=10$ hours and $\operatorname{Var}(S_B)=20$ hours$^2$. What is the squared coefficient of variation $C_s^2=\operatorname{Var}(S)/(\mathbb{E}[S])^2$ of the effective service time?

One machine serves red jobs at rate $\lambda_r=0.5$ and blue jobs at $\lambda_b=2.5$ per hour, with net service mean $\mathbb{E}[S_0]=0.25$ hour. Each batch of one colour needs a setup with $\mathbb{E}[R]=2$ hours; red batches hold $B_r=10$ jobs, blue $B_b=40$. Charging each job its effective service time, what is the load?

In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. Assume $\mathbb{E}[R]>0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)>0$, and let $C_0^2=\operatorname{Var}(S_0)/(\mathbb{E}[S_0])^2$. Since $\operatorname{Var}(S)\geq\operatorname{Var}(S_0)$, must the effective SCV satisfy $C_s^2\geq C_0^2$?
options: Yes: $\operatorname{Var}(S)\geq\operatorname{Var}(S_0)$ forces $C_s^2\geq C_0^2$.
Yes: $C_s^2=B\,C_{s,B}^2$, and this is at least $C_0^2$.
No: $C_s^2<C_0^2$ always, because $\mathbb{E}[S]>\mathbb{E}[S_0]$.
No: a deterministic setup gives $C_s^2<C_0^2$, a very variable one $C_s^2>C_0^2$.

questions.question: In a setup model, jobs are served in batches of $B\geq2$ jobs; each batch needs one setup time $R$ and then $B$ i.i.d. net service times $S_0$, independent of $R$. The effective service time is given $\operatorname{Var}(S)=\operatorname{Var}(S_B)/B$, not $\operatorname{Var}(S_B/B)=\operatorname{Var}(S_B)/B^2$. Which property is this choice designed to give?
options: $S$ is the job's net service plus $R/B$, whose variance is $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)+\operatorname{Var}(R)/B$.
The sum of $B$ independent copies of $S$ has the same mean and variance as $S_B$.
The per-job SCV equals the batch SCV, $C_s^2=C_{s,B}^2$, so spreading keeps the SCV.
$\operatorname{Var}(S)$ vanishes as $B$ grows, just like the setup share $\mathbb{E}[R]/B$.

questions.question: Batches of $B=8$ jobs need one setup $R$ ($\mathbb{E}[R]=1$ hour, $\operatorname{Var}(R)=\tfrac{1}{4}$) and eight i.i.d. net services $S_0$ ($\mathbb{E}[S_0]=\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)=\tfrac{1}{16}$), independent of $R$. Jobs arrive at $\lambda=2$ per hour, $C_a^2=1$. With the effective $S$, what is $\frac{C_a^2+C_s^2}{2}\cdot\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\cdot\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: $\tfrac{15}{16}\approx0.94$ hour
$\tfrac{9}{8}\approx1.13$ hours
$\tfrac{13}{16}\approx0.81$ hour

questions.question: Batches of $B=12$ jobs need one setup $R$ ($\mathbb{E}[R]=1.2$ hours, $\operatorname{Var}(R)=0.36$) and i.i.d. net services $S_0$ ($\mathbb{E}[S_0]=0.2$, $\operatorname{Var}(S_0)=0.04$), independent of $R$. Plan A halves every setup ($R$ becomes $R/2$); plan B keeps $R$ and sets $B=24$. How do the effective service times $S$ compare?
options: Equal $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and equal $\operatorname{Var}(S)=0.055$, since both halve the setup share.
Plan A has the smaller $\mathbb{E}[S]$, since it shortens every setup itself.
Equal $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.25$; plan A has the smaller $\operatorname{Var}(S)$, $0.0475$ against $0.055$.
Equal $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.25$; plan B has the smaller $\operatorname{Var}(S)$, $0.055$ against $0.07$.
